stances.claim: Justice Jose A. R. Melo -- 'Justice Pepe' -- was CJ's first SC friend, mentor through 'the little-known processes of the Court,' and principal wedding sponsor of CJ's daughter Marilen, a relationship grounded in shared Pampango heritage that persisted through judicial meetings here and abroad and weekend golf and tennis.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-bond disclosure (the friendship before the institutional tribute)

stances.claim: Melo deserves the four-word portrait CJ assigned him in 'Reforming the Judiciary' (2002): mild-mannered (gentle and fair yet firm in conviction, tolerant of dissent, free of self-importance), eloquent (through action, body language, gesture, and smile rather than flowery words), loyal (especially to friends on the shorter end of an argument), and open (transparent, 'read like a book,' loathed high-powered rhetoric).

Melo's pre-existing SC characterization -- 'the consensus builder of the Court and living barometer of its leanings and positions on various issues... respected by his colleagues for his objectivity, fairness, lucidity, and openness to new ideas and contrary views' -- captures the temperament that made him the right Comelec chair when GMA called him back to public service at age 76.

Melo's Comelec chairmanship (March 25, 2008 - Jan. 16, 2011) carried real reputational risk because he was succeeding the contract-invalidation trio of SC decisions that had caused 2004 and 2007 to be conducted manually, and he 'retired from the Court with an enviable record of performance with no backlog at all' -- yet he accepted the post, automated the 2010 presidential election under PCOS, installed Benigno Aquino III 'with nary a protest from his opponents,' and voluntarily retired early to give his successor planning time.

For 'daring the odds and succeeding,' Justice Pepe should be recognized as the 'Father of Automated Elections in the Philippines' -- a title CJ first conferred in his May 26, 2019 column and reiterates here as Melo's enduring institutional legacy.

notable_anecdotes: The Pampango-language detail -- CJ and Melo 'conversed in our native Pampango' even as they traveled with their spouses to judicial meetings abroad -- the linguistic intimacy that anchored a SC-judiciary friendship in a shared regional identity.
Melo as principal wedding sponsor of CJ's daughter Marilen on December 20, 1995 -- a specific family-life datum that converts the institutional tribute into a kin-bond disclosure.

The 85%-vs-15% Division-vs-En-Banc deliberation ratio -- 'about 85 percent of all decisions were deliberated and promulgated by the Divisions (and only 15 percent by the Banc)' -- Melo and CJ sharing a Division for seven of Melo's ten years made institutional observation up close.

Melo's aphorism on friendship: 'one did not need a friend when one was right. One needed a friend when one was wrong, to be consoled and empathized with while promising to do better next time' -- preserved verbatim as the philosophy behind 'loyal to a fault.'

The PCOS pre-election test-run failures -- 'some of the precinct count optical scan (PCOS) machines failed to read the ballots during their test runs' -- the operational mess Melo nonetheless converted into a successful 2010 installation of Aquino III 'with nary a protest from his opponents.'

Melo's voluntary early retirement on January 16, 2011 -- 'well ahead of his six-year term' -- to give his replacement sufficient time to plan the next polls, modeling the institutional-handover ethic CJ has celebrated repeatedly.

The recursive book-citation discipline: CJ quoting his own 1997 ('Justice and Faith,' p. 144) and 2002 ('Reforming the Judiciary') books verbatim, then his May 26, 2019 column -- the obituary as a curated archive of CJ's own prior assessments of Melo.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the obituary tribute for retired SC Justice Jose A. R. 'Pepe' Melo, who 'passed to the Great Beyond' on October 18, 2020 at age 88. Melo was President Fidel V. Ramos's first SC appointee on August 10, 1992, having previously served as 'much-admired presiding justice' of the Court of Appeals. He was CJ's 'first friend in the Court,' the mentor who patiently taught him 'the little-known processes,' and the principal wedding sponsor of CJ's daughter Marilen on December 20, 1995 -- a friendship anchored in their shared Pampango heritage that they continued to converse in even while traveling abroad for judicial meetings with their spouses. They served on the same SC Division for seven of Melo's ten years (where 85 percent of decisions were deliberated, against 15 percent En Banc), and played golf and tennis on weekends. CJ quotes himself from 'Justice and Faith' (1997, p. 144) on Melo as 'the consensus builder of the Court and living barometer of its leanings and positions on various issues... respected by his colleagues for his objectivity, fairness, lucidity, and openness to new ideas and contrary views,' and from 'Reforming the Judiciary' (2002) with the four-word portrait -- mild-mannered, eloquent, loyal, and open -- each elaborated in turn: mild-mannered meant gentle and fair yet firm in convictions and tolerant of dissent, free of bloated self-opinion ('he felt uncomfortable when praised'); eloquent meant through action, body language, facial expression, gesticulation, grin, and smile rather than 'flowery words or verbal flourishes'; loyal meant to country, Court, his wife Norma, his children Olivia Anne, Jaime Alberto, and Jorge Alfonso, and to friends -- 'especially... when his friend was on the shorter end of an argument' (Melo's aphorism: 'one did not need a friend when one was right. One needed a friend when one was wrong, to be consoled and empathized with while promising to do better next time'); and open meant transparent, 'read like a book,' loathing 'high-powered rhetoric and highfalutin words.' Six years after retiring from the SC, GMA called Melo back to public service on March 25, 2008 at age 76 as Comelec chair -- after the SC had invalidated three poll-agency contracts to automate the 2004 presidential election (causing 2004 and 2007 to be conducted manually). Under his 'gung-ho leadership' Comelec 'courageously automated the 2010 presidential election,' and despite PCOS machines failing test runs, the election installed Benigno Aquino III 'with nary a protest from his opponents.' Melo voluntarily retired from Comelec on January 16, 2011, 'well ahead of his six-year term,' to give his replacement planning time. Given the prior SC defeats and PCOS media criticism, CJ initially thought Justice Pepe 'risked too much in accepting the chairmanship' -- he had retired from the Court with 'an enviable record of performance with no backlog at all.' For 'daring the odds and succeeding,' CJ reiterates his May 26, 2019 designation that Melo should be recognized as the 'Father of Automated Elections in the Philippines.'
